title: Short day today: stocks close at 1 p.m.
text: Wall Street reopens this morning after Thanksgiving, but only for a half day. Stocks stop trading at 1 p.m. Eastern time. The prices on this page are still from Wednesday's close, because the market was shut on Thursday. Overnight, most stock markets in Asia went up, led by tech and AI companies. That can give U.S. tech stocks a lift at the open, but nothing is promised. Today is also Black Friday, so stores and online sellers like Amazon may get extra attention.

title: AI suppliers are still much further from their highs
text: The five AI supplier companies on our list (NVIDIA, Broadcom, TSMC, Vertiv and AMD) are, on average, about 40% below their highest price of the past year. The four AI giants (Alphabet, Amazon, Microsoft and Meta) are about 21% below on average. The suppliers also carry higher risk scores: about 6.7 out of 10, versus about 4.4 for the giants. Suppliers sell chips and equipment, so their sales can jump or drop quickly when the giants change their spending plans.

title: Online holiday shopping is off to a strong start
text: Adobe, which tracks online sales, says Americans spent $82.5 billion online from November 1 to 22. That is 9.1% more than the same days last year. Adobe expects about $12.9 billion of online spending on Black Friday alone. These are online sales only, and the Black Friday number is a forecast, not a final count. Strong shopping is usually a good sign for the economy and for Amazon.

title: A busy week for NVIDIA is coming
text: NVIDIA's CEO, Jensen Huang, is set to answer questions from lawmakers next week, in a private meeting with House committees on December 1 and a public Senate hearing on December 3. The Senate hearing is about rules that limit selling advanced chips to other countries. Big news from Washington can move NVIDIA, and other chip stocks often move with it.

title: Lesson 70: What is liquidity?
text: Liquidity means how easy it is to buy or sell something quickly without changing its price much. A popular stock like Microsoft is very liquid: millions of shares trade every day, so there is almost always someone ready to buy or sell. A rare baseball card is not very liquid: you may wait weeks for a buyer, or have to drop your price. Liquidity can change. On short holiday days like today, many traders take the day off. With fewer buyers and sellers, a few big orders can push prices more than usual. That is why one quiet day's move should not be read as a big signal. For long-term investors, liquidity mostly matters when you need your money fast.

title: What this update covers
text: Prices are from Wednesday, November 25, the last full trading day, because U.S. markets were closed Thursday for Thanksgiving. Risk scores and price scenarios use those prices. Analyst price targets are shown for NVIDIA, TSMC, AMD, Alphabet, Amazon, Microsoft, Meta, Lockheed Martin and GE Aerospace; the free data plan does not include them for Broadcom, Vertiv, Rocket Lab, Eli Lilly or Intuitive Surgical. The 10 year Treasury chart shows monthly averages through October. This is information for learning, not advice to buy or sell anything.
